Types of evidence

This section sets out the type of evidence which may be produced and factors which should be taken into account when considering it. The list of evidence is not exhaustive, and applicants can rely on any relevant evidence to support their application.

In the following table of possible supporting evidence, any piece of evidence marked conclusive is sufficient to meet the requirements of VDA 4.2. No further consideration of other evidence is required unless there is a counter allegation where you should refer to the Counter allegation section of this guidance.

When considering any other type of evidence in support of an in-country application for settlement under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse (VDA), you should consider the evidence in the round and, if the applicant provides information or evidence that, when considered in the round, indicates the account given by the applicant is, on the balance of probabilities, more likely than not, then VDA 4.2. is met.

When considering evidence in support of an application for out of country settlement under Appendix VDA, you should consider the evidence in the round and, if the applicant provides information or evidence that, when considered in the round, indicates the account given by the applicant is reasonably likely to be true, the account should be accepted. As transnational marriage abandonment is a recognised form of domestic abuse then this would be sufficient evidence to meet VDA 4.2. and VDA 4.3.

Where limited evidence is available, in particular where the only evidence available is a statement from the applicant, consideration should be given to any reasons provided for the lack of documentary evidence in support of the application. In particular, where any reasons arise from or otherwise relate to the abusive relationship or situation the applicant is or was in.

Where an applicant indicates that evidence in support of their application might be available through records available to or requested by the Home Office, for example: UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI), His Majesty’s (HM) Passport Office (HMPO) and police records, consideration should be given to making reasonable enquiries on behalf of the applicant on a case-by-case basis and in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and other data sharing protocols.

In assessing evidence of domestic abuse and abandonment, the same weight should be given to evidence of disclosures and reports of abuse and abandonment made by victims to family, organisations, or professionals abroad.

When looking at the evidence in the round, you must consider and detail both positive and negative factors. The failure to do so is likely to be unlawful:

‘In essence, the decision […] is a list of factors which undermine the Claimant’s account rather than an assessment of the indicators which might constitute reasonable grounds for suspecting that the Claimant was a victim of trafficking. It would appear that on the basis of the discrepancies, gaps and the adverse inferences that could be drawn from the Claimant’s account, the Defendant simply rejected her account and concluded that her credibility was sufficiently limited to justify finding no reasonable grounds to suspect that the Claimant could be a victim of trafficking’ (R (on the application of Wen) v. SSHD, [2019] EWHC 2104 (Admin) at [62[vi)].

Criminal conviction

Weight of evidence

Conclusive: A criminal conviction which relates to domestic abuse is proof that the domestic abuse occurred on the dates cited.

If the applicant has also been convicted of a criminal offence which is related to domestic abuse, decision makers must consider how far this should be considered, including the general grounds for refusal. However, you should be aware of the context of the relationship and that convictions may not mean the applicant is not also a victim under Appendix VDA.

Additional information required

Criminal convictions require a higher standard of proof (beyond reasonable doubt) than immigration decisions (on the balance of probabilities) an acquittal must not be taken as proof that domestic abuse did not occur on a balance of probabilities.

Police caution

Weight of evidence

Conclusive: Accepting a caution is an admission of guilt and can be accepted as evidence that domestic abuse occurred on the dates cited.

If the applicant has also accepted a caution which is related to domestic abuse, decision makers must consider how far this should be considered in the overall context of the relationship.

Order or finding in civil court

Weight of evidence

Conclusive: If a judge has found that domestic abuse occurred, this will have been on the balance of probabilities and can be accepted as definitive proof of domestic abuse for the purposes of Appendix VDA.

Admissions by the perpetrator can also be made during proceedings which can be the basis on which a Non-Molestation Order or Occupation Order can be made and that, like a judicial finding, this should be accepted as conclusive proof of domestic abuse.

If there is no finding of fact recorded on the order or otherwise in the proceedings, it should not be classed as conclusive proof that domestic abuse has taken place, but it can be very compelling evidence that domestic abuse has taken place.

Additional information required

This is a non-exhaustive list but court documents or findings could include those found in the Domestic Abuse Statutory Guidance which provides a table of protective orders at Annex D.

Police logs and social service reports may be useful additional evidence and give details that will assist in deciding how much weight to give such an order.

Multi-agency risk assessment conference (MARAC) referral confirmed by any person who is a member of a MARAC

Weight of evidence

An assessment should be made of whether the MARAC should be judged as conclusive on the information contained in the document. For example: if the applicant is in imminent danger or there is an element of concern for the individual. This will be most likely in cases rated ‘high risk’.

The threshold for referring cases to MARAC is not always applied consistently.

Additional information required

Full reports may not be available or disclosable. Applicants may include correspondence from the MARAC, or a professional involved in the referral confirming that the MARAC referral has been made and providing details as to why.

Charging decision from CPS

Weight of evidence

Conclusive: The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decides to charge someone with a criminal offence when it is satisfied that there is sufficient evidence to provide a realistic prospect of conviction and that it is in the public interest to do so.

The ‘realistic prospect of conviction’ test is a legal view given by the CPS on the balance of probabilities. Therefore, this should be given the same weight as an order in civil court and no further enquiries are needed.

Personal statement from the applicant

Weight of evidence

Although all evidence provided should be considered under Appendix VDA, most applicants will choose to provide a personal statement or account. The weight given to this statement should be considered in the round as detailed in this guidance and as per the evidential requirements for out of country applicants bearing in mind their specific circumstances.

Decision-makers must take into consideration the impact of trauma and abuse as well as other factors which may impact an applicant’s account such as feelings of shame, fear or mistrust of authorities or language barriers.

Decision-makers must also take into consideration the inherent limitations that may exist when third parties, such as the police or medical professionals, create records of their interaction with the applicant.

Where the account provided is reasonably detailed, consistent and plausible, consideration should be given to whether the applicant’s account may be sufficient evidence, in particular where persuasive reasons are given for the absence of further or other evidence.

The applicant’s account must be considered with other information and evidence provided, in the round.

Additional information required

Information provided in the statement that appears to contradict other evidence should be considered further to identify any reasons for the apparent discrepancy so that the decision-maker can determine whether the apparent contradiction is material to their assessment. This may require the decision-maker to ask the applicant about the discrepancy.

Domestic violence protection order (DVPO) and Domestic Violence Protection Notices (DVPN).

Weight of evidence

DVPOs issued by a court should be treated as conclusive evidence that domestic abuse has occurred.

A DVPO can only be made where the court is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the perpetrator has been violent towards, or has threatened violence towards, an associated person, and that the order is necessary to protect that person from further violence or threats of violence (section 28, Crime and Security Act 2010).

Given this statutory threshold, a DVPO represents a judicial finding that domestic abuse has taken place. Where an applicant provides a valid DVPO relating to them, caseworkers must accept this as conclusive evidence for the purposes of Appendix Victims of Domestic Abuse. No further corroborating evidence or enquiries are required in relation to the abuse itself.

DVPNs are issued by the police under section 24 of the Crime and Security Act 2010. The legal threshold for issuing a DVPN is that the police have reasonable grounds for believing that the perpetrator has been violent towards, or has threatened violence towards, an associated person.

Where an applicant relies on a DVPN that has not been followed by the making of a DVPO, this evidence does not reflect a judicial determination and may not, on its own, be sufficient to establish that domestic abuse has occurred for the purposes of Appendix Victims of Domestic Abuse.

Caseworkers should note that where a DVPN is issued, the police are required to apply to the court for a DVPO (section 27, Crime and Security Act 2010). If a DVPO is subsequently made, it should be treated as conclusive evidence in line with the guidance above.

Additional information required

Caseworkers may request further information where appropriate, for example from the police, to understand the context and outcome of the DVPN. This applies only to DVPNs and not to DVPOs.

Domestic Abuse Protection Orders (DAPO) and Domestic Abuse Protection Notices (DAPN)

Weight of evidence

DAPOs made by a court under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 should be treated as conclusive evidence that domestic abuse has occurred.

A court may make a DAPO only where it is satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the perpetrator has been abusive towards a person aged 16 or over to whom they are personally connected, and that the order is necessary and proportionate to protect that person from domestic abuse or the risk of domestic abuse (section 32, Domestic Abuse Act 2021).

Given this statutory threshold, a DAPO reflects a judicial determination that domestic abuse has taken place. Where an applicant provides a valid DAPO relating to them, caseworkers must accept this as conclusive evidence for the purposes of Appendix Victims of Domestic Abuse. No further corroborating evidence or enquiries are required in relation to the abuse itself.

DAPNs are issued by the police under section 22 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021. The legal threshold for issuing a DAPN is that the police have reasonable grounds for believing that a person has been abusive towards another person.

Where an applicant relies on a DAPN that has not been followed by the making of a DAPO, this evidence does not reflect a judicial determination and may not, on its own, be sufficient to establish that domestic abuse has occurred for the purposes of Appendix Victims of Domestic Abuse.

Caseworkers should note that where a DAPN is issued, the police are required to apply to the court for a DAPO (section 28(3), Domestic Abuse Act 2021). Where a DAPO is subsequently made, it should be treated as conclusive evidence in line with the guidance above.

Additional information required

Caseworkers may request further information where appropriate, for example from the police, to understand the circumstances leading to the issuing of the DAPN and any subsequent action taken. This applies only to DAPNs and not DAPOs.

Ex parte orders (a decision made by a judge without requiring all the parties to be present) for example ex parte molestation order or occupation order

Weight of evidence

Ex parte orders are made by the court based on perceived risk to the applicant. As both sides have not been heard, they are not compelling evidence that domestic abuse has occurred.

Additional information required

Ex parte orders are made on the evidence of one party only, although once the order is made, the other party can challenge it. If there is a follow up hearing, decision makers must obtain the details of any further orders, challenges or undertakings.

Prohibited steps orders, contact orders, Specific Issue Orders, disclosure of whereabouts orders, port alert order, securing a child’s passport order, order to recover a child, as well as High Court orders using the court’s inherent jurisdiction

Weight of evidence

Conclusive: If there has been a finding of fact regarding domestic abuse after a hearing in the court.

If a judge has found that domestic abuse occurred, this will have been on the balance of probabilities and can be accepted as conclusive evidence of domestic abuse for the purposes of Appendix VDA.

If there is no finding of fact and there is evidence that domestic abuse was a factor in granting the order, then this will be compelling evidence subject to the details of the abuse provided.

These orders regulate the relationship between children and parents. Orders of this type can also be made in cases where a relationship has broken down for reasons other than domestic abuse which would be less compelling evidence.

Additional information required

Decision makers must establish that an allegation of domestic abuse was a factor in the decision.

It is important to recognise that a judgment with a finding of fact may be relevant evidence and not necessarily the court order itself. In family court cases there may be a schedule of findings of fact for example. It does not always follow that particular orders are made after findings of fact.

Letter from social services, or welfare officer connected to HM Armed Forces

Weight of evidence

Can be accepted as compelling evidence if the letter confirms that social services have assessed the applicant themselves and has the experience to consider them a victim of domestic abuse.

Additional information required

These reports normally also include evidence from any children and may include a Children and Family Court Advisory and Support Service (CAFCASS) assessment.

The letter should also provide details as to what support the applicant is being offered as a result of the domestic abuse or relationship breakdown.

Letters and other assessments from a domestic abuse professional working within a charity or public sector organisation providing domestic abuse services confirming that they have assessed the applicant as being a victim of domestic abuse.

Letter or assessment should detail support being provided, and if no additional support has been provided explain why this is (for example, where a refuge is full).

Weight of evidence

Can be accepted as very compelling evidence of domestic abuse, depending on the content, when it is a charity or public sector organisation providing domestic abuse services that is:

listed in the Women’s Aid Directory

listed in the Respect Services Directory

part of a Community Safety Partnership

is otherwise providing domestic abuse services within or on behalf of a local authority.

Evidence will be considered very compelling where it includes a summary of a detailed professional assessment (for example, interviews, risk assessments, professional opinions, summaries of other associated services or third-party involvement.)

Letters and other assessments can be compelling when from a domestic abuse professional working within a charity or public sector organisation that is not included on the Women’s Aid or Respect directories and does not provide services within or via a local authority or Community Safety Partnership. How much weight is given will depend on the content of the evidence; the training, experience and expertise of the domestic abuse professional; the nature and extent of their organisation’s support of the applicant; and the proven track record of the organisation in providing domestic abuse support services, especially in the context of by and for organisations.

This evidence may fail to reach the evidential threshold where there is very compelling counter evidence that damages the credibility of the applicant.

Additional information required

Evidence can be accepted without additional information or enquiries when the domestic abuse service is found in the:

Women’s Aid Directory

Respect Services Directory

Evidence can usually be accepted when the domestic abuse service is provided via a Community Safety Partnership or within or on behalf of a local authority. You may need to search the relevant area to confirm this is the case. For example, here is the relevant page for London.

When a charity or public sector organisation providing domestic abuse services is acting in support of an applicant but is not included in one of the above directories and does not provide services via a local authority or Community Safety Partnership you may need to undertake further enquiries.

Where a charity submits evidence and is not found in any of the above you can search the relevant charity register. You should confirm on the relevant charity register that providing services for victims of domestic abuse and / or violence against women and girls is consistent with the charity’s stated purpose and activities.

Depending on the contents of the letter, you may need to follow up to confirm that the charity or public sector organisation has made a professional assessment based on relevant training, expertise or experience as a domestic abuse professional, the nature and extent of their support of the applicant, as well as the proven track record of the organisation in providing domestic abuse support services. You may need to ask for further detail on how the conclusion was reached, and / or to clarify that it is not merely relaying the applicant’s account.

If there is no evidence, even after contacting them, that the support is from a charity or public sector organisation providing domestic abuse services then you should consider the evidence within the next section of this table

Letters and other assessments from individuals or organisations that cannot be considered in the above section of this table confirming that, while acting in their professional capacity or otherwise in the course of their business, they have assessed the applicant as being a victim of domestic abuse.

Letter or assessment should detail support being provided, and if no additional support has been provided explain why this is (for example, where a service is full).

Weight of evidence

This evidence must be considered with other information and evidence provided and in the round.

Evidence can vary from compelling to not compelling depending on the individual or organisation’s training and qualifications, experience and expertise in working with victims of domestic abuse, the nature and extent of the individual or organisation’s support of the applicant, the proven track record of the organisation in working with victims of domestic abuse, and the content of the evidence provided.

The following individuals or organisations are more likely to provide compelling evidence:

a person or organisation who is regulated, .

an organisation that provides publicly funded domestic abuse services with funding from local authorities, central government or other public bodies, for example, Police and Crime Commissioner

a not-for-profit organisation that provides domestic abuse services with funding from charitable trusts and foundations

an organisation that has a proven track record of providing specialist domestic abuse services

a person or organisation that has an active caseload supporting victims of domestic abuse

a person who is currently a MARAC practitioner

Factors that would likely cause evidence to be less compelling:

an individual or organisation working for profit whose work with the applicant is limited to providing evidence in support of their application and there is no evidence the individual or organisation is otherwise engaged in providing domestic abuse support services.

an individual that lacks qualification / experience / expertise or an organisation that lacks a proven track record in supporting victims of domestic abuse

the evidence repeats the applicant’s account and does not detail their professional assessment (for example, interviews, risk assessments, professional opinions, summaries of other associated services or third-party involvement.)

Individuals or organisations that are unregulated by professional bodies and have charged the applicant for the evidence they have provided should be subject to the greatest scrutiny. Factors that would likely undermine the weight of their evidence include:

Companies House records show that mandatory reporting under the Companies Act 2006 – such as providing accounts or confirmation statements – is overdue

Companies House records show the organisation has outstanding charges against it

the organisation or person does not respond to Home Office enquiries or questions in a reasonable timeframe (30 days) or withdraws its previous supporting evidence when asked to give further details

the organisation does not appear to have any public presence that suggests it supports victims of domestic abuse

the organisation or person provides no plausible reason for why the applicant sought its particular services and is unable to confirm whether they have met the applicant in person

Home Office records show the organisation or person regularly supports people who are making Appendix VDA applications even though the nature of their business (for example, the provision of housing) does not explain why they are providing evidential support to victims of domestic abuse.

Additional information required

You must search Companies House to confirm the nature of the organisation that has submitted evidence and whether it exists.

If the organisation is not registered on Companies House, you should enquire as to the nature of their business (for example, sole trader or partnership) and request evidence of this.

It is also worth searching for the organisation’s public presence such as its website to ascertain whether the organisation works with victims of domestic abuse.

As a matter of routine, you do not need to write out for further details from individuals or organisations who have completed letters or other assessments while acting in their professional capacity or otherwise in the course of their business and that cannot be considered in the above section of this table. It is for them to demonstrate in the evidence they provide that they have qualifications, experience and expertise in working with victims of domestic abuse and / or that their organisation has a proven track record of working with victims of domestic abuse.

However, if you choose to do so you may wish to further enquire on the following (this list is not exhaustive, and you may make any reasonable enquiries based on the information given in the application and / or information known to the Home Office):

the basis of them offering an opinion or assessment of the applicant as a victim of domestic abuse with particular regard to whether they are regulated professionals, providing publicly funded domestic abuse services, have an active caseload supporting victims of domestic abuse or are currently a MARAC practitioner.

the nature of their relationship with the applicant, how they were introduced, whether they have met in person and how often, and what support or services have been provided beyond the provision of the evidence

whether they have charged the applicant for any services either directly or received funds indirectly when supporting the applicant

the regularity with which they support applicants making applications under Appendix VDA, and why that is if it does not appear to be a core function or purpose of their business or organisation

Any other reasonable enquiries about the nature of their business, its operations and interaction with the applicant and Home Office.

Domestic Abuse Stalking and Honour Based Violence (DASH) risk assessment or Domestic Abuse Risk Assessment (DARA).

Weight of evidence

DASH (Domestic Abuse, Stalking and Honour Based Violence) is a risk assessment used by practitioners who work with victims of domestic abuse.

The risk levels are standard, medium and high. Victims who are assessed as high risk will meet the threshold for referral to a Multi-Agency Risk Assessment Conference (MARAC).

The weight of evidence placed on a DASH or DARA should follow the same guidance as for other types of letters or assessments outlined in the previous 2 entries.

Where the DASH or DARA is submitted with a further letter of support or assessment, it will be more compelling than when submitted by itself.

The criteria for the high-risk threshold to be met are: 14 or more yes answers on the DASH checklist, escalation in frequency and severity of abuse or professional judgement of the practitioner.

The DARA is a tool for police first responders which may be used instead of DASH as it contains additional questions to clarify the situation for children.

In all these scenarios, risk assessments must be looked at in the round and in the context of other available evidence.

Additional information required

DASH risk assessments must be considered with other information and evidence provided, in the round.

Where the victim has been assessed as at high risk then case workers should seek the outcome of the MARAC, where a MARAC referral has been made.

Letter or statement from an independent or connected witness

Weight of evidence

The weight given to this type of evidence depends on whether it can be verified that:

they witnessed an incident of domestic abuse first hand

have no personal stake in the case, for example, they are not related to the applicant

You should still consider a statement where the person has not witnessed the abuse ‘first hand’. In cases involving coercive or controlling behaviour, abuse may be psychological, financial, sexual, or ongoing, and may not be visible to others.

The nature of the relationship of friend or family is relevant to weight, but consideration must be given to what the person says or has seen which may support the claim. It should be considered whether the person merely repeats the account given by the applicant or whether they have witnessed any of the abuse or after-effects of the abuse first hand.

Evidence from independent or connected witnesses who observed indirect indicators of abuse (for example, injuries, distress, isolation, or controlling behaviour) should be assessed in the round alongside all other evidence.

Additional information required

The difficulty of evidencing that there is no possible relationship or connection between the applicant and any independent witness will reduce the weight given to this type of evidence unless any corroborating evidence demonstrating the witness’ independence can be provided.

Arrest

Weight of evidence

The police have the power to arrest anyone who they suspect has committed a criminal offence and they have reasonable grounds for believing that the arrest is necessary.

To arrest someone for domestic abuse, the police will have to have some basis to suspect that the person has committed an offence. However, this is different from having sufficient evidence to charge that person, and the fact that someone has been arrested for domestic abuse is not compelling evidence on its own that it has occurred.

It should be noted that a person may be investigated for an offence even if they have not been arrested. For example: if someone will agree voluntarily to attend the police station to be interviewed in relation to an offence, the police may not consider it necessary to arrest them.

Additional information required

Following an arrest and if their enquiries are ongoing the police must release someone on bail. Conditions could be attached to the grant of bail. Although the available evidence is considered when deciding whether to impose bail conditions, it is not the principal consideration. The decision to release someone on conditional bail does not, on its own, provide evidence on the balance of probabilities that domestic abuse has or has not occurred.

Further information should be sought from the police in relation to the progress of their investigation and outstanding enquiries.

Applicants can provide crime reference numbers with their application and decision makers can make enquiries with the police and request the relevant reports and confirmation of what action was taken.

Police‑Held Information (Clare’s Law / Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme).

In Scotland it is known as the Disclosure Scheme for Domestic Abuse Scotland (DSDAS) and in Northern Ireland it is known as the Domestic Violence and Abuse Disclosure Scheme (DVDAS).

Weight of evidence

Within a witness statement an applicant may reveal they have received a disclosure under the Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme (Clare’s Law) from a particular police force for their own protection.

During this disclosure, the police can inform someone their partner or ex‑partner has a history of violent or abusive offending.

Depending on the details provided, this disclosure could provide compelling evidence alongside other police reports.

Additional information required

Clare’s Law disclosures are provided verbally, so no written document is issued. However, the underlying information is held by the police, so you will need to verify this directly with the appropriate force.

Interim order

Weight of evidence

An interim order may be imposed during a civil case when the hearing has started but the case is not yet concluded.

Additional information required

The weight to be attached to an interim order will depend on how far the case has progressed and the terms of the order.

Undertaking to court

Weight of evidence

Undertakings can be given by either or both parties to settle a case.

An undertaking (for example: not to approach the applicant) is not compelling evidence if no admission of guilt has been made.

If an admission of guilt in relation to domestic abuse has formed part of the undertaking, then this can be considered conclusive evidence.

In some cases, an applicant may have given a cross‑undertaking (where both parties give undertakings). This can happen for practical reasons, such as to avoid a contested hearing, legal costs, or delay.

A cross‑undertaking does not necessarily mean that abuse did not occur or that the applicant was equally responsible.

Undertakings often include broad or neutral terms (for example, directing both parties not to contact or harass each other). These terms may not reflect the full history or nature of the abuse and may offer limited protection to the victim.

You must assess any undertaking in the round, alongside the applicant’s statement and all other available evidence.

Additional information required

Unless there is a clear admission of guilt, ask for further details of the court proceedings.

Further evidence, for example police reports, medical reports and professional assessments may also be required to understand the weight this evidence should be afforded in your decision.

Where an applicant has given an undertaking that appears inconsistent with, or may undermine, their account of domestic abuse, you should seek further information or clarification.

This may include:

the context in which the undertaking was given

whether the applicant had access to legal advice or advocacy support at the time

whether the undertaking was given to avoid a contested hearing or further legal action

whether the terms of the undertaking limited the applicant’s ability to raise or evidence abuse

Police report of attendance at domestic abuse incident

Weight of evidence

The police have a duty to respond to calls of possible criminal offences or to protect the public. A report of attendance at an alleged incident is not itself proof of domestic abuse.

The weight given to this type of evidence will be highly dependent on its contents and the circumstances of the victim.

Evidence of police follow up action or supporting evidence, for example medical evidence, will generally be required to add weight to this type of evidence.

However, it may provide a contemporaneous record supporting the applicant’s report and account of events, or it might show a pattern of police reports about the applicant being a victim or the perpetrator being an abuser, regardless of whether or not further police action takes place.

Additional information required

Further information should be sought from the police in relation to the progress of their investigation and outstanding enquiries.

Medical reports or other evidence from medical professionals (including psychiatrists) confirming injuries, treatment or health conditions consistent with domestic abuse

Weight of evidence

Can be considered compelling evidence where the report confirms injuries or conditions consistent with domestic abuse or reveals a pattern of injuries or reports from the applicant about domestic abuse.

GP records or other medical reports may be considered as corroborating evidence because they come from an independent source. They may show that there were contemporaneous complaints which may corroborate in terms of content and timing. Any medication or treatment may also be supportive evidence

The weight given to this type of evidence will be highly dependent on its contents, in certain circumstances it could be viewed as conclusive.

Medical evidence can be relevant even where records do not contain detailed notes about domestic abuse.

Victims of domestic abuse may present to medical professionals with physical or psychological symptoms such as anxiety, depression, stress, or unexplained pain, without disclosing the underlying cause. In some cases, abuse may be mis‑recorded or described in general terms (for example as a ‘family problem’ or a mental health condition).

The absence of an explicit or detailed reference to domestic abuse in medical records does not mean that abuse did not occur. Medical consultations are often brief and focused on treating symptoms rather than recording wider social or safeguarding issues.

Psychiatrist reports will be less compelling when it only consists of a one-off session that simply reflects the applicant’s account. Where there is evidence of follow up sessions or ongoing support this should be given more weight.

Medical evidence should therefore be assessed in the round, alongside the applicant’s statement and all other available evidence.

However, this type of evidence will be less compelling when the medical report or notes simply reflect the account reported by the applicant although weight should be given to any insight from an experienced medical professional and the timings of the disclosures.

Additional information required

The medical report should be provided by the GP or medical professional who provided the consultation and give details of any hospital or other treatment needed.

The absence of medical evidence should not be taken as evidence that abuse did not occur. Victims may lack GP registration, treatment history, or records because of the abuse.

Power of arrest

Weight of evidence

A power of arrest is routinely included in a non-molestation order. The wording is standard and does not indicate the evidential weight of the order.

An occupation order does not automatically have a power of arrest attached. Under section 47(2) of the Family Law Act 1996 this provides for a power of arrest only if it appears to the court that the respondent has used or threatened violence against the applicant or a relevant child. Given this threshold, a power of arrest attached to an occupation order should be given considerably more evidential weight.

Letter report or statement from official source, such as an advice agency or refuge repeating applicant’s account without confirming that applicant has been assessed as, or is being treated as, the victim of domestic abuse.

Weight of evidence

Not compelling evidence on its own but must be considered in light of the rest of the evidence.

Additional information required

Decision makers should confirm that the organisation has not formally assessed applicant as the victim of domestic abuse and is not offering support on that basis.

Letter, statement, email, text or photos repeating applicant’s account of domestic abuse

Weight of evidence

Must be considered in the round with the rest of the evidence.

Contemporaneous emails, texts, social media conversations or photos should be considered if they outline incidences of abuse or back up other evidence provided. For example: a conversation about an injury with a family member ahead of a medical report from a GP.

Evidence that repeats the applicant’s account will add little weight to that given to the applicant’s statement.

The nature of the relationship of friend or family is relevant to weight, but consideration must be given to what the person says or has seen which may support the claim. It should be considered whether the person merely repeats the account given by the applicant or whether they have witnessed any of the abuse or after-effects of the abuse first hand. Any correspondence with one or more of the abusive parties that reveals threatening or abusive behaviour may also be compelling if the source of the communications can be verified.

Screenshots of video, emails, audio files, photos or text messages will be less compelling as they may provide just a snapshot of interactions between the relevant parties, and they have been selected for submission by the applicant.

Advances in AI mean that, where there is no other evidence, consideration should be given to whether there is anything to indicate that emails, texts, social media conversations or photographs relied upon could have been edited or otherwise altered using AI.

Additional information required

Photos can be linked to any medical reports that may have been submitted.

A mobile phone bill addressed to the perpetrator may link them to a phone number.

The Home Office cannot accept video or audio files so, if an applicant wishes to submit this type of evidence, they must do so in an acceptable format such as screenshots or transcripts.

Consideration of applications

Applicants under this route may be vulnerable and affected by the trauma they have experienced as victims of domestic abuse. Some applicants may still be at risk of abuse including those who apply while still cohabiting with an alleged abuser. You must deal with cases sensitively, flexibly and cooperatively giving applicants support to demonstrate their eligibility where this is needed.

Where an applicant does not fall to be refused on suitability grounds, but the evidence provided is insufficient to determine eligibility for settlement under Appendix VDA, you must attempt to contact the applicant to request further information, following the process set out below:

you must make at least 2 attempts in total over a minimum of 8 weeks to contact the applicant

your contacts should set out clearly what further information or evidence you are seeking

your contacts should explain how the applicant should respond

contacts should be by email or letter using the applicant’s contact details or those of a legal representative if they have asked you to communicate with a representative - however, you should avoid contacting an applicant at their address when they are still residing with their perpetrator

you may in addition call or text at the same time as sending an email or letter

you must give at least 28 calendar days for a response to the first contact

28 calendar days are counted from the date an email is sent or a letter is received - where the attempted contact is by letter sent by first class post, you may assume delivery on the second business day after the date of postage

if the applicant informs you within that 28-calendar day period that they require further time to provide information or evidence, you must agree to a reasonable extension of time where you are satisfied that there is good reason to do so in the particular circumstances of the case

if there is no response from the applicant by the deadline, including any extended deadline, you must contact the applicant a second time by email or letter - you may in addition call or text at the same time as sending an email or letter

you must give at least 28 calendar days for a response to the second contact. If the applicant informs within that period that they require further time to provide information or evidence, you must agree to a reasonable extension of time where you are satisfied that there is good reason to do so in the particular circumstances of the case

in either the first or second contact, you may provide longer than 28 calendar days where, following consultation with your senior case - worker, you are satisfied that there is good reason to do so in the particular circumstances of the case

you can exceed that number of attempts at contact where, following consultation with your senior case - worker, you are satisfied that there is good reason to do so in the particular circumstances of the case

all attempts at contact must be recorded

if the applicant makes clear that they are unable or unwilling to provide more information or evidence, you must decide the application based on all the information and evidence before you

Once the final deadline you have given the applicant to provide more information or evidence (or to contact you to discuss this) has passed, you must consider and decide the application based on all the information and evidence before you, including any further information or evidence the applicant has provided.

Throughout this process of engagement with the applicant, you may exercise discretion in their favour where appropriate, to minimise administrative burdens and show sensitivity towards vulnerable applicants. Consideration should be given to any reasons provided for a lack of documentary evidence, in particular where any reasons given arise from or otherwise relate to the abusive relationship the applicant is or was in and consideration should be given to exercising discretion to accept the applicant’s eligibility on the evidence available.

In consultation with a senior case - worker, if necessary and appropriate, you can make reasonable enquiries on behalf of the applicant on a case-by-case basis and in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and other data sharing protocols, where an applicant is having difficulty in proving their eligibility.’

Pending criminal prosecutions, cautions and proceedings

This page tells you about how to deal with applications where the alleged abuser has a criminal case pending or a caution or other proceedings.

Pending criminal prosecutions

Where an alleged abuser has been charged and there is a criminal prosecution pending, the applicant should provide as much information as possible, including any documentary evidence that has been given to them as the victim of a crime.

The applicant may not be able to provide documentary evidence of a decision to prosecute. Where this is the case, you should make reasonable enquiries on the applicant’s behalf to obtain this evidence where confirmation of the prosecution is considered necessary to decide the application.

Applicants may not have a comprehensive understanding of the UK criminal justice system and may not have been given information by the police or Crime Prosecution Service (CPS), so may not be able to explain the current status of any criminal proceedings. Where an applicant is unable to provide documentary evidence or detailed information about any criminal proceedings, but indicates that there has been police involvement, consideration should be given to making enquiries with the police or otherwise making reasonable enquiries on behalf of the applicant on a case-by-case basis and in line with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and other data sharing protocols.

You can continue to assess and decide the application but must remember that the burden of proof in criminal cases is ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ whereas the standard of proof in immigration cases is ‘on the balance of probabilities’ and, in transnational marriage abandonment applications under this route is ‘reasonable degree of likelihood.’

Police cautions

The applicant may not be able to provide documentary evidence the police have issued a caution against the alleged abuser.

Where the applicant alleges a caution has been issued and this information has not already been provided in the application, you must ask them for details of the alleged abusers:

full name

date of birth

nationality

address (both at the time of the incident and at the time of the application, if different and if known)

You must also ask them for details of the date, time and place where the incident took place.

Using these details, you must confirm with the Criminal Records Office (CRO) of the police force covering the area where the incident took place.

Delay in civil cases

You should only consider delaying a decision on the application until the outcome of a civil hearing if you are genuinely unable to grant settlement based on the evidence already before you.

In such a case, you should only delay a decision pending the outcome of a civil hearing if you have both:

confirmation from the court that the case is listed to be heard

the date the case is due to be heard

Court proceedings can be lengthy and you should monitor progress of proceedings where reasonable. You should write out to the applicant asking for information on any changes to the hearing date and further information once the hearing has taken place.

Applicants should be asked to provide as much information as possible. However, note that there are restrictions, under section 12 of the Administration of Justice Act 1960, relating to disclosure of documents from Family Court proceedings which may mean an applicant cannot provide relevant information or evidence regarding proceedings in the Family Court without the court’s permission.

Court orders

This page tells you about the details included in a court order.

Terms used in court orders

Applicant’s name: this should be the same name as the person who requests permission to stay on the basis of domestic abuse.

Respondent’s name: this should be the applicant’s partner’s name or a member of their family. If the respondent’s name does not come within the category of a family member, or you are not sure, you must consult your senior case worker.

It may not always be the case that an order has an applicant or respondent’s name on it. For example: a female genital mutilation (FGM) Protection Order made in respect of a child will have the name of the child on it as well as those who are a risk to the child in respect of whom the order has been made.

It is not necessarily the case that the applicant’s name will be the same person who is applying for permission. A victim of domestic abuse could be a respondent to an application, for example a child arrangements order and a judgment could still be made including findings of domestic abuse against the perpetrator.

Layout of court orders

The orders generally follow this layout:

judge’s name and court address

paragraph on whether the order is made on an urgent basis / if so, why

paragraph which indicates whether the order is made without notice (ex-parte)

paragraph about any ‘undertakings’ if any are made:

undertakings, by one or both parties, may be given to a court instead of proceeding to a full hearing for a final non-molestation order, or together with the issue of a final non-molestation order where ‘no finding of fact’ is made

this means there is not necessarily a ‘finding of fact’ on the allegations

an undertaking is not an admission of guilt unless it specifically says so

‘important notice to the respondent’ ‘it is ordered that:’ followed by details of what the respondent must or must not do

detail about period for which the order is to remain in force

‘power of arrest’ - reference to attachment

‘no finding of fact’ (on the allegations by the applicant) - may be detailed at the start or end of the order

‘notice of further hearing’ (interim orders) - may be ‘headed up’ in this way, or may just provide details of time / date / place of further hearing

costs

Counter allegations

Introduction to counter allegations

This section provides guidance to support fair and informed decisions on applications involving counter allegations, ensuring victims and their dependants are protected. This section also applies to counter allegations in transnational marriage abandonment (TMA) cases.

Glossary of key terms

Applicant: refers to the person who submitted the Appendix VDA application.

Counter allegations: counter allegations refer to any information that challenges or contradicts the applicant’s account of domestic abuse. This may come from the sponsor (or a member of the sponsor’s family), social services, Home Office records, the police, or other agencies. Counter allegations can involve a denial that the abuse occurred or a claim that the sponsor rather than the applicant is the victim.

You should recognise that counter allegations may be false or may not reflect the full context of the relationship. Counter allegations are a common tactic used by perpetrators to maintain power and control. For example, by attempting to force the alleged victim back into the relationship or disrupt their efforts to secure an independent immigration status. A counter allegation may also be used to shift blame or avoid the consequences of being found, or suspected, to be a perpetrator of domestic abuse.

There may be circumstances where the perpetrator will accuse the victim of having mental health issues or other difficulties and use this to suggest that the abuse did not occur. However, it is also important to acknowledge that counter allegations may have merit and may be supported by corroborating evidence. Caseworkers should therefore consider all allegations and assess them against the available evidence.

This guidance first explains the concept of the primary perpetrator and primary victim. It then sets out the decision‑making process for 3 different counter allegation scenarios.

Identifying the primary victim and primary perpetrator

The approach of identifying a primary victim and a primary perpetrator recognises that, in most domestic abuse cases, one person is the primary perpetrator (using abusive behaviour to gain or maintain power and control), while the other is the primary victim (primarily responding, resisting, or trying to protect themselves). Mutual abuse, where both people use abusive behaviour or violence to the same extent and with the same intent, is very rare. Understanding this approach can support your decision making and your consideration of the evidence available to you. You should refrain from framing relationships as ‘toxic’ as there can be a perception that in a ‘toxic relationship’ both parties are to blame. Instead, focus on whether the relevant behaviour constitutes domestic abuse as defined in the Domestic Abuse Act 2021.

You should look at the overall pattern of behaviour and the power dynamics in the relationship rather than relying on isolated incidents. The primary perpetrator is not necessarily the person who initiated the most recent incident. Victims are not always passive; they may respond in a retaliatory or protective way. Consider whether the primary victim’s use of force was to protect themselves or another person, such as a child. Recognise that resistance violence has different motivations than violence from perpetrators. It may occur in contexts of safety planning (getting to the safest place immediately after violence), survival or dignity (‘I will not be treated like this’).

It is important to note that domestic abuse is a gendered issue, with men much more likely to be the primary perpetrators and women more likely to be the primary victim. Men can also be victims, but women are substantially more likely to be. In LGBTQIA+ relationships you should not assume that these gendered patterns apply.

Decision making

The Immigration Rules do not specify any mandatory evidence or documents to be submitted with a counter allegation. Using the Types of evidence section of this guidance, you must weigh the evidence presented by each side and decide whether you are satisfied, on the balance of probabilities (or, in cases of transnational marriage abandonment, to a reasonable degree of likelihood), that domestic abuse has occurred and which account is more credible.

Where information has been provided by a former sponsor or the police with an explicit request that it is not disclosed or where disclosure could place the sponsor or another individual at risk or compromise police activity, the details must not be disclosed unless confirmation has been obtained from the police or relevant authority that disclosure is safe and appropriate.

In making a decision, you must only use disclosable evidence from either the applicant or the counter claimant. If the evidence is not disclosable, you cannot consider it as part of your decision.

The following section explains the decision-making process for 3 different counter allegation scenarios.

Scenario 1: The applicant presents conclusive evidence

If the applicant presents conclusive evidence (as referenced in the evidence table of this guidance document) that they were the victim of domestic abuse, the counter allegation should be disregarded.

All points raised in the conclusive evidence’s additional information column also apply here and may impact the final decision.

In the rare circumstance where both parties present conclusive evidence, you should seek advice from the Domestic Abuse Migrant policy team via email.

Scenario 2: The applicant reaches the evidence threshold

Disregard the counter allegation if the applicant reaches the evidential threshold and the counter allegation provides only a personal statement.

Scenario 3: Covers 3 scenarios requiring a similar approach

Scenario 3 covers the following 3 scenarios which require a similar approach:

the counter allegation includes compelling or corroborating evidence

the counter allegation and the applicant present limited evidence

the counter allegation includes conclusive evidence

The focus should remain on assessing the strength and credibility of the applicant’s account, rather than attempting to find an ‘absolute truth’ within the conflicting narratives.

Where a counter allegation refers to contact with the police, social services, MARAC or another agency but no evidence has been provided, you should make every attempt to verify this information independently. If the public body / agency does not consent to this information being disclosed, you cannot take it into account when making your decision.

Assess the relationship dynamics and patterns of abuse. Use the Identifying the primary victim and primary perpetrator section to recognise the primary victim or perpetrator.

Where you are minded to refuse an application, in whole or in part, on the basis of a counter allegation, procedural fairness requires that the applicant is given a meaningful opportunity to respond before a final decision is made.

You must put a clear and proportionate summary of the counter allegation to the applicant and invite a response. The applicant must be given the opportunity to provide further information, explanation or evidence.

You may only notify the applicant of a counter allegation where you have consent to disclose the evidence and / or the counter allegation is already known to the applicant (for example, because it relates to an arrest, police attendance, charge or conviction).

This step is essential because conduct linked to retaliation, self-defence or resistance may be criminalised or admitted by the applicant and, without proper context, could wrongly be treated as determinative or conclusive evidence against them. The applicant’s response must then be considered alongside all evidence before reaching a decision.

Weigh all evidence and decide which account, on the balance of probabilities (or reasonable degree of likelihood for TMA), is more credible. If you determine the applicant’s account to be more credible than the counter allegation, you must submit your proposal to the Grade 7 before the counter allegation can be disregarded. Your proposal must be clearly explained and evidenced.

If you determine the counter allegation to be more credible than the applicant’s account, you must submit your proposal to refuse the Appendix VDA application to the Grade 7. Your proposal must be clearly explained and evidenced.

If your decision remains unclear seek advice from a senior caseworker or the Domestic Abuse Migrant Policy team via email.

The counter allegation guidance cannot cover all possible scenarios because every situation, perpetrator and victim are different. If you are unsure about your decision, contact a senior caseworker or the Domestic Abuse Migrant Policy team via email.

3C leave

There is no requirement for an applicant to hold valid permission to apply under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse (VDA).

This page tells you when section 3C of the Immigration Act 1971 applies.

The purpose of section 3C is to prevent a person who makes an in-time application to extend their permission from becoming an overstayer while they are awaiting a decision on that application or any appeal and, if their application under Appendix VDA has been refused, while any administrative review they are entitled to is pending.

Pending decision on application

A person will have permission extended by section 3C if:

they have permission to enter or remain in the UK

they apply to the Secretary of State for variation of their permission

the application for variation is made before their permission expires

their permission expires without the application for variation having been decided

the application for variation is neither decided nor withdrawn

Pending administrative review

Section 3C extends a person’s current permission during any period when:

an administrative review could be sought

the administrative review is pending, that is to say it has not been determined

no new application for permission has been made

For further information see guidance on 3C leave.

Grant or refuse settlement

This page tells you how to grant or refuse applications for settlement under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse (VDA).

Grant settlement

You must grant settlement if a person meets all the requirements of Appendix VDA and confirm this in writing.

In-country applicants should be granted settlement with the endorsement Domestic Violence – ILR.

Out of country applicants should be granted settlement with the endorsement Settlement Victim of Domestic Abuse – ILE.

Refuse settlement

You should normally refuse settlement if any of the requirements of Appendix VDA are not met notwithstanding the discretion allowed to case - workers in the above sections.

A detailed explanation must always be given in cases where you do not consider the evidence provided is sufficient to demonstrate that domestic abuse has taken place.

When refusing an EU, other EEA or Swiss citizen, or their family member, with extant pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme (EUSS) who obtained permission under the Migrant Victims of Domestic Abuse Concession, you must note in your refusal letter that the person continues to hold pre-settled status.

Reconsiderations

This page explains under what circumstances a case may be reconsidered.

Applications should normally only be reconsidered following:

instruction from the court

advice from Government Legal Department (GLD) or policy

request from the Administrative Review team

reconsideration request from the applicant or their legal representatives

For example: the Administrative Review team may request a review of the decision because you may have omitted to include an assessment of a piece of evidence in your original decision. You must re-consider all the evidence submitted with the original application or during the Administrative Review, fully address all the information and issue a new decision.

You should allow introduction of new evidence at a reconsideration stage, especially so if the new evidence clearly shows that the applicant does now meet the rules under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse (VDA). The new decision will need to address the new evidence raised, as well as that originally submitted. The revised decision will need to address the issues raised by GLD or policy colleagues in order sufficiently to address any legal challenge. You should seek further advice from the chief case – worker (CCW) or deputy chief case - worker (CCW) if necessary.

The applicant or their legal representative must be contacted during the reconsideration process to advise of the likely timescale for a reconsideration decision to be made.

Cancellation

This page tells you what additional action you may take when you refuse an application under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse (VDA).

In non-EUSS cases you must consider a referral concerning cancellation of permission when you refuse an application from someone who meets Appendix VDA 4.1. (permission under a relevant category) but does not meet Appendix VDA 4.2. (relationship breakdown) and who has over one month permission to stay or enter the UK as a:

spouse

civil partner

same-sex partner

unmarried partner

This is because they now cease to meet the rules under which they were granted permission to enter or stay in the UK but ensures that those who apply but do not satisfy Appendix VDA 4.1. because they do not have permission in a qualifying category, for example: because they have permission under the Hong Kong (BNO) route do not find their permission unlawfully curtailed.

Consideration of curtailment of EUSS limited leave

The Status Review Unit (SRU) is the team responsible for EUSS curtailment decisions.

Referrals for curtailment of EUSS limited leave (also known as pre-settled status), including from Immigration, Compliance and Enforcement (ICE) teams, must be made to the SRU in line with section ‘Consideration of curtailment of EUSS limited leave or EUSS family permit leave to enter’ in the guidance Cancellation and curtailment of permission.
